summary:
Borno stands under the national framework of Nigeria, but its criminalisation of same-sex conduct rests on Borno's own legislation as well as federal law. Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law.

Borno State's own statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000), gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001 and signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000, makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the state under Section 3. Section 7 provides that any person who engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death. Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement, and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

The UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states, of which Borno is one, and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women. The maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment. The note includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police.

Borno enacted its own state Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, in addition to its secular morality law. The parallel Sharia layer for Borno therefore rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than on federal or umbrella coverage. No operation date or gazette has been identified for this code, and the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the sourcebook's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes.
tangentialFactors:
Borno's death penalty for same-sex conduct is enacted in state legislation, not only imported from the federal SSMPA or an umbrella Shari'a framework, which distinguishes its exposure profile from states relying solely on national law.

The sourcebook's incomplete annotation of Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 reflects a documentation gap rather than an absence of law: the statute was obtained after the volume's annotation was finished.
localsOnly:
Residents of Borno face prosecution under three overlapping layers: the federal SSMPA, Borno's own 2000 morality statute carrying a death penalty for same-sex intercourse, and Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001. Jurisdiction over morality offences under the state statute lies with Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts.

The hisbah, or morality police, operate in Borno as in other northern states, and the UK Home Office note documents their role alongside formal Sharia enforcement mechanisms.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Borno-specific enforcement incidents, arrests, or violence against trans or gender-nonconforming people are documented in this inventory; the record establishes the legal framework only.

The operation date and gazette for Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001 remain unidentified in the sourcebook, and the full text has not been independently annotated by that project.

Whether the death penalty under Borno's 2000 statute has been carried out for same-sex conduct is not sourced here.
